unit.can_do_en: say what is wrong and ask for something for it.

judge.reason: Moi/hei and mä/minä are only register differences.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Mul on päänsärkyy. Onks teil jotain siihen?
lines.text_kirja: Minulla on päänsärkyä. Onko teillä jotain siihen?
lines.gloss_en: I have a headache. Do you have something for it?

judge.reason: Same content: headache and asking if they have something for it; only spoken forms differ.

lines.speaker: Laura
lines.gloss_en: Yes. This is a good painkiller.

judge.reason: Tää/tämä is a register difference; same statement.

lines.speaker: Laura
lines.gloss_en: One tablet three times a day.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Do I need a prescription for it?

judge.reason: Tarviiks siihen reseptii and Tarvitaanko siihen reseptiä both ask whether a prescription is needed; the written form is passive but means the same.

lines.speaker: Laura
lines.text_puhe: Ei tarvii. Se maksaa kuus euroo.
lines.text_kirja: Ei tarvita. Se maksaa kuusi euroa.

judge.reason: Ei tarvii/ei tarvita both mean not needed; kuus euroo/kuusi euroa is six euros in both.
Mä/minä and kiitti/kiitos are register differences.

forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Voida, can, with -n for 'I': voin.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Minä with -lla. With on it means 'I have'. Speech shortens it to mul.
The form of olla, to be, for he, she or it. People say it the same way.
The partitive singular is used for an ache you have: päänsärky becomes päänsärkyä. Speech says päänsärkyy.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: On with -ko to ask a question. Speech often says -ks: onks.
Te, you, with -llä: teillä. With on it means 'you have'. Speech shortens -llä to -l: teillä becomes teil.
The partitive singular of jokin 'something': jotain. People say it the same way.
The illative singular of se 'it': siihen, 'into it, for it'. People say it the same way.
Speech shortens tämä to tää. Books write tämä.

After kuinka 'how' you use the partitive singular of moni: monta, 'how many'.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech drops the final i: yksi becomes yks.

After a number above one, the noun takes the partitive singular: kolme kertaa, 'three times'.
The inessive singular gives 'per': kolme kertaa päivässä, 'three times in a day'.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, passive, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: The passive tarvitaan 'one needs' takes -ko to ask. Speech says tarviiks instead.
The partitive singular after tarvita: resepti becomes reseptiä. Speech changes the last ä to i: reseptii.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. People say it the same way.
Ei tarvita means 'no one needs it'. Speech says ei tarvii.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Maksaa, to cost or pay. With se, 'it', the verb ends in a long vowel: maksaa.
Speech drops the final i: kuusi becomes kuus.
After a number the noun takes the partitive: neljä euroa. Speech turns -oa into -oo.
Ottaa, to take, with -n for 'I'. The tt becomes t: otan.
Se with -n when the whole thing is the object: kirjoittaa sen.
Kiitti is the everyday spoken thanks. Books write kiitos.
